# STIR

STIR is Nick Milo's model of the four universal ways we organize and remember things: **S**pace, **T**ime, **I**mportance and **R**elatedness. The guiding question it supports is "What would Future Me like to see?"

## Origin
Milo started from the five ways to organize information in Richard Saul Wurman's *Information Anxiety* (see Information Anxiety (book)): location, alphabet, time, category, hierarchy. He felt that, in a linked-notes world, relatedness was the most important principle and was only weakly covered by "hierarchy", so he reframed the set as STIR.

## Recall
In Milo's workshops the practical claim is that you are most likely to retrieve a thing when all four elements are represented. Mapping notes such as Maps of Content are valuable partly because they supply space and relatedness.

## Mapping to ACE
Space is Atlas, Time is Calendar, Importance is Efforts, and Relatedness is the set of links across them. See ACE Folder Framework (LYT).

## Digital versus analog
- A daily digital note organizes by time; recency makes the latest items feel important, but that fades. The fix is to link the item to a related note, ideally a high-gravity MOC, which acts as a dependable space.
- A paper notebook organizes by space and short-term importance (recency bias); once a page is out of sight it is effectively lost. Milo suggests digitizing only the bits you want to keep developing so they can relate to your other ideas. He frames the best creative work as a blend of analog and digital.
